captions: July twenty-second — another huge earnings day,
with more than sixty companies reporting.
But today was a day of extremes.
On the same day,
one stock hit a record high on a stellar result,
while an oil giant posted a nearly four-thousand-crore loss.
And it all ties back to one thing —
the crude spike that crashed the market today.
Let's break down who won, who lost, and why.
Remember — all comparisons are year-on-year,
and this is information analysis, not investment advice.
Let's start with today's story in three numbers.
IndusInd Bank — net profit one thousand thirty-seven crore,
up seventy-two percent.
A big beat.
Nestle India — profit nine hundred fifty-nine crore,
up forty-eight percent,
sending the stock to a fifty-two-week high.
But B-P-C-L — the oil giant —
swung to a loss of nearly four thousand crore.
Two big beats and a shock loss, all on the same day.
And the dividing line between them is crude oil.
Let's see who was on which side.
First, the winners.
IndusInd Bank posted a net profit of one thousand thirty-seven crore,
up seventy-two percent.
Its net interest income was strong,
and asset quality improved,
with bad loans falling to three point two five percent.
That's reassuring for the whole private-bank space,
which had been under a cloud.
Nestle India was the star — profit up forty-eight percent,
revenue up twenty-five percent,
sending the stock to a fifty-two-week high.
Then a fascinating one — Eternal, the parent of Zomato.
Its revenue jumped a huge one hundred eighty-two percent and profit rose two hundred sixty-eight percent.
And yet the stock fell.
Why?
We'll explain that in a moment.
The read-through —
F-M-C-G and private banks shrugged off crude.
But the day truly belonged to oil, as we'll see next.
Now the losers — and the theme is crude.
B-P-C-L, the oil marketing giant,
swung to a loss of nearly four thousand crore,
versus a six-thousand-crore profit a year ago.
When crude spikes suddenly,
oil marketers take inventory and margin losses —
and that's exactly what happened.
H-P-C-L told the same story,
also slipping into a loss on the crude and inventory hit.
Doctor Reddy's was a different kind of loser —
its profit fell sixty-nine percent,
but that was due to US price erosion in pharma,
a separate pressure, not crude.
And here's the big connection —
the very same crude spike that crashed the market today is what pushed these oil marketers into the red.
The market's fear and these losses are two sides of one coin.
So what are the lessons?
Three of them.
First, and the most important —
Eternal grew its profit two hundred sixty-eight percent,
yet the stock fell.
Why?
Because it missed what analysts expected —
ninety-two crore versus around two hundred fifty-eight crore.
The market pays for beating expectations,
not just for growth.
Second —
the oil marketers posting losses does not mean they're broken.
A sudden crude spike causes one-off inventory and margin losses that often reverse when prices stabilise.
Third — never assume all results move together.
On this one day,
Nestle hit a record high while B-P-C-L posted a four-thousand-crore loss.
Sector and expectations decide the reaction —
not the headline number alone.
Finally,
five things to remember when reading any earnings day.
One — always compare against expectations,
not just last year.
Eternal grew profit two hundred sixty-eight percent and still fell,
because it missed estimates.
Two — sector context decides the reaction.
Today, crude helped no oil marketer,
but F-M-C-G and banks thrived.
Three — oil marketer losses are often crude-inventory driven.
Check whether it's a one-off before you judge the business.
Four — a genuine record profit, like Nestle's,
can send a stock straight to a fifty-two-week high.
Five — one quarter is never the whole story.
Watch consistency over several quarters before you conclude anything.
July twenty-second earnings, at a glance.
The beats — IndusInd Bank up seventy-two percent,
and Nestle up forty-eight percent to a record high.
The losses —
B-P-C-L down nearly four thousand crore and H-P-C-L in the red,
as the crude spike crushed the oil marketers.
Doctor Reddy's profit fell sixty-nine percent on US pricing pressure.
And the lesson of the day —
Eternal grew profit two hundred sixty-eight percent but missed estimates,
so its stock fell.
It's not the number —
it's the number versus what was expected,
and the sector it's in.
This information is aggregated from public sources —
for analysis only, not investment advice.
Thanks for watching.
